items.title: Recursion uses stack space
items.claim: A naive recursive Fibonacci function fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) for n=50 will:

options.text: Take roughly 2^50 (~10^15) function calls and either run for hours or exhaust the stack/timeout — naive recursion has exponential complexity even though the iteration is linear
Always crash with a syntax error

items.reveal:
Naive recursive Fibonacci recomputes the same values exponentially many times. Memoisation (caching computed values) or dynamic programming reduces it to O(n) time and O(n) or O(1) space.

Tail-call optimisation (TCO) is a compiler technique to reuse stack frames for tail-recursive calls; Scheme requires it, OCaml supports it, Python doesn't. Functional languages often rely on TCO to make recursion as cheap as iteration.
items.why: Recursion is elegant but not free. Stack depth and redundant work are common pitfalls that can be fixed without abandoning the technique.

items.title: GPL and copyleft
items.claim: Richard Stallman launched the GNU project in 1983 and wrote the GPL licence. What property defines 'copyleft'?

options.text: Software must be free of charge
Derivative works must also be distributed under the same licence
Only the original author may modify it

items.reveal:
Copyleft uses copyright law to ensure freedoms are preserved downstream. GPL v2 (1991) and v3 (2007) are the most widely deployed copyleft licences.

Permissive licences (MIT, BSD, Apache) take a different approach by not requiring share-alike.
items.why: Software freedom is a legal architecture, not just a technical one.
